reviewer: Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), independent blind reviewer D

items.evidence: Para 3: 'fledglings of the short-tailed shearwater embark on their maiden migratory flights guided by the moon and stars, only to be fatally disoriented by coastal roadway lighting, crashing into traffic or concrete walls.' Option d ('confuses young birds on their first flight, so they end up among roads and buildings') paraphrases this as maiden flight = first flight, disoriented = confuses, traffic/concrete walls = roads and buildings.
issues: Only one option is defensible. b is a good, deliberate distractor: it takes the delayed-foraging and predator harm from the sugar glider/microbat sentence and pins it on the wrong animal. It rewards careful attribution and cannot be defended for shearwaters.

a, c and e have no support in the passage. e ('blinds them permanently') is a fair misreading trap for 'disoriented', but it is clearly wrong. a and c are weak, easily ruled out, so in practice this is a 2-way choice for a careful reader.

Mild length cue: d is the longest option (~15 words against 9-13). b is close enough (~12) that the cue is weak. d paraphrases the passage rather than copying it, so verbatim matching does not give it away.
'end up among roads and buildings' is softer than the passage ('fatally disoriented ... crashing into'). It is still accurate, not misleading.
No factual problems: grounding of short-tailed shearwater fledglings by coastal lighting (e.g. Phillip Island) is well documented. The language is fine for Year 6.
Difficulty: at the lower-middle end for scholarship. It is literal retrieval with one attribution trap (b). That is acceptable for an early item in the set.
items.fix: Optional polish only. Shorten d to cut the length cue, e.g. 'It confuses them on their first flight, so they fly into roads and walls.' Optionally swap a or c for a closer distractor tied to the passage, e.g. 'It hides the moon and stars, so they cannot leave the island at all.'

items.evidence: Para 4: 'Local councils can replace unshielded lamps that cast glare in every direction with downward-facing hooded fixtures that direct illumination exclusively where pedestrians step.' Option b ('Fitting hooded fixtures so street lamps shine only towards the ground') matches this.
issues: Only one option is defensible. a turns two recommendations upside down: blue-white instead of warm-amber, and every direction instead of downward. c is contradicted by 'does not require plunging our communities into perilous darkness'. d and e go against para 2's argument that glare and unshielded floodlights are not the answer.

No clash with the warm-amber LED recommendation, because no option offers it. Do not add an amber option later: the passage does not clearly say whether that step belongs to councils, which would create a two-answer risk.

Mild lexical cue: b reuses the key phrase 'hooded fixtures' from the passage. The rest is paraphrased ('shine only towards the ground'), so it is not near-verbatim. Option lengths are balanced (8-11 words, with a as long as b).
The distractors are distinct, but all except c simply reverse the author's view, so a reader who has the gist eliminates them quickly.
Difficulty: easy for Year 6 scholarship. It is direct retrieval from one sentence. This is acceptable as a lead-in item but adds little discrimination.
items.fix: Optional: to remove the keyword match and lift difficulty, reword b as 'Fitting covers so that street lamps point their light downwards' and replace d or e with a closer distractor, e.g. 'Moving street lamps away from footpaths so pedestrians walk in darkness'. Neither change is needed to pass.
